marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q001.takeaway: Complementary nucleotides on opposite DNA strands pair through hydrogen bonds; each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q001.displayText:
Complementary nucleotides on opposite DNA strands pair through hydrogen bonds; each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine.

The true statement about DNA is that the nucleotide of one strand binds with the nucleotide of
the opposite strand.
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymeric molcule containing genetic information. It is a
double-stranded molecule consisting of nucleotide pairs. Each nucleotide pair includes one purine
and one pyrimidine. The nucleotide of one strand binds with the nucleotide of the opposite strand
by hydrogen bonds.
Other options:
Option B: The information from DNA is copied in the form of mRNA.
===== PDF PAGE 390 =====
Option D: Cytosine and uracil differ by one amino group.
emphasis: Complementary nucleotides on opposite DNA strands pair through hydrogen bonds; each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine

rationales.a: A purine–purine pair would be too wide for the uniform DNA helix; canonical pairs combine a purine with a pyrimidine.
rationales.b: DNA information is transcribed into RNA, with mRNA carrying protein-coding information; tRNA is an adaptor in translation.
rationales.d: Cytosine and uracil differ by a methyl group on the base, not by the presence of ribose, which is in RNA nucleotides.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 381; explanation p. 389,390.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q003.takeaway: Chargaff pairing gives A = T = 28%; the remaining 44% is G + C, so cytosine is 22%.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q003.displayText:
Chargaff pairing gives A = T = 28%; the remaining 44% is G + C, so cytosine is 22%.

The percentage of cytosine in DNA will be 22%.
According to Chargaff's rule in cellular DNA, regardless of species,
A=TandG=C
Purines = Pyrimidines i.e. AtG = C+T.
In the question it is given that thymine is 28%, therefore adenine is also 28%. So, adenine +
thymine = 56% and guanine + cytosine = 44%. Since guanine = cytosine, the percentage of
cytosine = 44/2 = 22%.
===== PDF PAGE 391 =====
emphasis: Chargaff pairing gives A = T = 28%; the remaining 44% is G + C, so cytosine is 22%

rationales.b: Thymine is 28%, and in double-stranded DNA adenine must also be 28%, so cytosine cannot be 28%.
rationales.c: With A + T totaling 56%, G + C totals 44%; equal G and C make cytosine 22%, not 36%.
rationales.d: 44% is the combined G plus C fraction, not cytosine alone.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q004.displayText:
B-DNA is the prevalent physiological form; A-DNA is favored by low humidity/high salt and Z-DNA is left-handed.

The correct statement is that B-DNA is the physiologically most common form.
There are 6 types of DNA- A, B, C, D, E and Z. All are right-handed except Z-DNA. Z-DNA is a
left-handed double helix in 5' end of chromosome and has phosphodiester backbone in a zigzag
form. A-DNA is found in conditions with low humidity and high salt concentration. B-DNA is the
physiologically most common form. It is found in conditions with high humidity and low salt
concentration.

emphasis: B-DNA is the prevalent physiological form; A-DNA is favored by low humidity/high salt and Z-DNA is left-handed

rationales.a: Z-DNA is left-handed, so calling it right-handed reverses its defining helix orientation.
rationales.b: High salt and low humidity favor A-DNA rather than B-DNA.
rationales.c: A-DNA is favored by low humidity and high salt, the opposite of the condition stated.

H1 is not a histone found in nucleosomes.
Chromatin is formed by nucleosomes, which are composed of DNA wound around an octameric
complex ofthistone molecules. They contain four major types of histones: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
Histones are a small family of closely related basic protein composed of arginine and lysine. H3
and H4 form a tetramer while H2A and H2B form dimers; these histone oligomers associate to
form the histone octamer. These four core histones are subject to at least six types of covalent
modification or post-translational modifications - acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation,
ADP-ribosylation, monoubiquitylation and sumoylation.
Hi histone is seen in the linker region between nucleosomes and is bound loosely to the
nucleosome.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q010.displayText:
The listed chromosome features are all correct: centromeres contain repeats, telomeres have TTAGGG repeats, and each chromatid has one dsDNA molecule.

All of the given statements are correct.
===== PDF PAGE 394 =====
Chomosomes can be visualised during metaphase of mitosis. At this point, they are duplicated
with two-fold symmetry. The duplicated, identical sister chromatids are connected at the
centromere. Each sister chromatid consists of a single dsDNA moleule. The centromere is an
adenine-thymine (A-T) - rich region containing repeated DNA sequence. The ends of each
chromosome contain structures called telomeres, which have a variable number of repeats of the
sequence 5'-TTAGGG-3'. Telomere shortening is associated with aging and malignant
transformation.

DNA polymerase I is an enzyme involved in DNA replication. It has polymerase activity along
with both 3'° 5'and5'° 3' exonuclease activity. When the 5'°  3' exonuclease domain is
removed, the remaining fragment is called Klenow fragment. It retains the polymerization and
proofreading activities of DNA polymerase I.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q015.takeaway: DNA replication is template-directed, semiconservative, bidirectional and semidiscontinuous; DNA polymerase requires a primer.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q015.displayText:
DNA replication is template-directed, semiconservative, bidirectional and semidiscontinuous; DNA polymerase requires a primer.

DNA replication is not template independent.
DNA replication occurs in S-phase of cell cycle. It is semi-conservative, semi-discontinuous
and bidirectional. DNA strands separate and each acts as a template strand on which new
complementary strand is synthesized. RNA primer is required. The new strand is synthesized
always in 5'-3' direction and thus, the synthesis of DNA in both strands is not the same.

rationales.a: Helicase continues strand separation after initiation; DnaA/origin-binding protein first recognizes the origin and initiates local opening.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q018.takeaway: Eukaryotic replication protein A binds single-stranded DNA to prevent reannealing and protect it from nucleases.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q018.displayText:
Eukaryotic replication protein A binds single-stranded DNA to prevent reannealing and protect it from nucleases.

Replication protein-A prevents strands from reannealing during the process of DNA replication.
Replication protein-A is a type of ssDNA-binding protein (SSB). During DNA replication, it binds
to the ssDNA generated by helicases. It shifts the equilibrium between dsDNA and ssDNA in the
direction of ssDNA and thus preve ts reannealing of strands. It also protects the ssDNA from
degradation by nucleases.
Option A: Helicase unwinds the DNA template at the replication fork.
Option B: DNA topoisomerases create a single- or double-stranded break in the helix to add or
remove supercoils.
Option D: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond within a strand of
double-stranded DNA.
===== PDF PAGE 399 =====
emphasis: Eukaryotic replication protein A binds single-stranded DNA to prevent reannealing and protect it from nucleases

rationales.a: Helicase unwinds the duplex; RPA binds the resulting single-stranded DNA rather than unwinding it.
rationales.b: Topoisomerases create transient strand breaks to relieve supercoils, not RPA.
rationales.d: DNA ligase seals nicks by forming phosphodiester bonds; RPA stabilizes ssDNA.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 385; explanation p. 398,399.
